### 4.1.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Faced with the reality of the collapse of the consensus requirement due to the penetration of autonomous agents, civil law scholarship must neither surrender to dogmatic despair nor remain trapped in past romanticism. What is required is a radical yet measured doctrinal reconstruction capable of bridging the gap between the normative text of Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) and the socio-technological dynamics of the 21st century. This reconstruction begins by expanding the doctrinal interpretation of defects of will traditionally recognized in the civil law tradition—namely *dwaling* (mistake / error), *bedrog* (fraud / deceit), and *bedreiging* (duress)—and integrating them with the doctrines of undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) and the exploitation of vulnerability that have evolved in modern jurisprudence. In the era of autonomous agents, fraud (*bedrog*) no longer requires verbal falsehoods uttered by a flesh-and-blood deceiver; it can be executed autonomously by lines of programmed code that systematically conceal material information or distort the victim's perception through the personalization of reality on screen displays.

Furthermore, the concept of *dwaling* or mistake must be redefined to encompass what may be termed an *algorithmically induced mistake*—a condition in which a contracting party suffers a misconception regarding the substance of an agreement not through their own ignorance, but because the information architecture presented by an autonomous agent has been manipulatively curated to induce this distortion of reality. It is precisely here that digital consumer protection doctrines and modern legal instruments—such as the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) and high-level regulations like the *EU Artificial Intelligence Act* (particularly Article 5 concerning prohibited manipulative practices that undermine substantive autonomy, and Article 50 regarding AI interaction transparency)—must be integrated into the conventional system of civil law interpretation. When an agreement is formed through the exploitation of cognitive vulnerabilities powered by artificial intelligence, that agreement must be qualified as containing a fundamental defect of will, resulting in the voidability (*vernietigbaar*) of the contract before a court of law.

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in the digital age demands a reaffirmation that legal intent (whether viewed through *wilswil* or a modified *verklaringstheorie*) must be assessed substantively rather than merely formalistically. Courts and legal practitioners must possess the courage to pierce the veil of digital formality—penetrating dazzling user interfaces and intricate lines of code—to examine whether a reasonable equilibrium of autonomy existed at the moment the consensus was secured. If it is proven that one party’s autonomous agent employed subliminal persuasion techniques, affective exploitation, or the manipulation of cognitive fatigue to coerce consensus, civil law is duty-bound to serve as a protective shield restoring the rights of the aggrieved subject. Ultimately, this doctrinal reconstruction serves as the final bastion in the defense of human dignity: an intellectual and normative endeavor to ensure that technological progress is never permitted to reduce human beings from their status as free legal subjects to mere computational objects controlled by algorithmic shadows.
